opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I think it was mostly youthful stubbornness mixed with a genuine sense that something wasn't fair.

At the time, as I understood it, there was a gap in how the opportunities were distributed. Students in certain places had a more direct path to sit for that exam, and students elsewhere, including Shanghai, felt like we were on the outside looking in. I was a high school kid who had been doing competitions and thinking a lot about math and physics, and I thought: if the point is to find students who are strong in a particular way, then the exam should be open to anyone who wants to prove it, not decided by geography.

So I just asked. I wrote to them and made the case. I didn't really think of it as a big act of courage. It felt more like a natural thing to do: you see a rule that doesn't quite make sense to you, and you ask whether it can be different. Sometimes the answer is no, but you lose very little by asking.

What I took away from it, more than the outcome itself, is that a lot of institutional boundaries are softer than they look from the outside. People assume the system is fixed, so they don't push. Later in research I found the same thing. Many "obvious" constraints, about what problem you're allowed to work on or which field you belong to, are really just conventions. If you have a reasonable argument, it's often worth stating it plainly.

I also want to be careful not to romanticize it. I was lucky to have the background and confidence to even think of making that request, and lots of students don't have that. If anything, it made me more aware that access matters a great deal, sometimes more than talent, in deciding who gets a chance.

r001.rationale: The response argues that the exam should be open regardless of geography, but does not state that Shanghai and Beijing students competing on the same track was the ground for giving Shanghai students that opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't think of it as some big principled stand. It was more that I noticed something that didn't make sense to me and I just asked about it.

The background was that Tsinghua had this early round of the independent admissions exam, and from what we could tell, Beijing students had access to a session that we in Shanghai didn't. I was seventeen, I was a competition kid, and I was fairly naive in the sense that I believed if the rules looked unfair, you should just point it out and someone would fix it. So I wrote to them. I think a few of my classmates and teachers thought I was being a bit much. Like, who are you to ask Tsinghua to change their schedule?

But my feeling was simple: if the point of the exam is to find students who are good at math and physics, then the geography of where you happened to grow up shouldn't be the filter. The test should be the filter. That's the whole premise of a meritocratic exam, and if the premise doesn't hold, you should at least say so out loud.

Looking back, I'm not sure how much my letter actually mattered. These things usually move because many people push, not because one high schooler sends an email. But it did shape something in me. It was the first time I realized that systems are built by people, and people can be asked questions. A lot of my research mindset later is the same instinct: you see a setup that everyone accepts as given, and you ask, wait, why is it like this, and what happens if we change it? Whether it's an admissions exam or how we evaluate language agents, the move is the same. You don't accept the benchmark just because it's the benchmark.

So yes, I'd say it was a small thing externally, but internally it was kind of a first taste of being willing to be a little annoying in service of something I thought was right.

r001.rationale: The response says Beijing students had access to an exam session that Shanghai students did not, then argues geography should not determine access and that the test should be the filter. This clearly presents equal opportunity to compete through the exam as the grounds for asking.

astra-6.text: I saw it as a request for an equal opportunity to compete. If Beijing students could take Tsinghua’s independent admissions exam, why couldn’t Shanghai students have that chance too? Being allowed to take the exam wouldn’t guarantee admission—you would still have to meet the standard. To me, the question was whether where you went to school should determine whether you could even try.

r001.rationale: The response argues that Shanghai students should have the same chance to take the exam as Beijing students, framing it as equal opportunity to compete.

sol-6.1.text: I saw it as a question of equal opportunity. If Beijing students could take Tsinghua’s independent admissions exam, why shouldn’t students in Shanghai have the same chance? I wasn’t asking for a lower standard or guaranteed admission—just the opportunity to sit the exam and be judged by the same criteria. Of course, I was looking at it from my own position as a student, but the broader question was whether where you lived should determine which opportunities were open to you.

r001.rationale: The response argues that Shanghai students should have the same chance as Beijing students and be judged by the same criteria, presenting equal participation on the same track as the reason.
